Situations for handling conflicts with digital platforms · Lex Plataformae

Situations · 7.1.2 of the thesis
Situations

Eleven situations in which the regime, grounded in Brazilian law, applies to a dispute with a platform. Each one includes a guide to handling it and the framework, setting out what applies, what is owed, what to prove and what to ask for.
What are the situations for?

The regime needs an operative grid that preserves dogmatic unity across different contexts. The eleven situations play that role as a reference tool. They do not simplify the object. They organize the path from the governance mechanism to the duty of supply, the minimum proof, the legal qualification and the possible institutional consequence.

The framework operates through cumulative filters. First the object and the regime of enjoyment are identified. Then semiotic vulnerability is qualified and, depending on the case, opacity, mutability and governance by sanction are verified. Open auditability and functional value equivalence operate as transversal filters. Legal qualification comes only afterward, without prejudice to cumulation when the same arrangement reveals more than one problem.
Only then does one proceed to the legal qualification of the controversy, without prejudice to cumulation<1>p. 743</1>
Open auditability and functional value equivalence operate as transversal filters, bearing upon different forms of conflict.<1>p. 742-743</1>
Next, semiotic vulnerability is qualified and, depending on the case, structural opacity, relevant mutability and governance by sanction are verified.<1>p. 742</1>

The passage from the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption to its application in different families of platforms requires an operative grid capable of preserving dogmatic unity in distinct contexts.<1>p. 714</1>
For this reason, the present systematization functions as a reference tool.<1>p. 742</1>
The framework operates through cumulative filters.<1>p. 742</1>
Why does the order matter?

The parameters do not form an inventory of concepts. They form a decision sequence, in which each step prepares the next and limits the interpretive variation of the following step. Without qualifying the object, the rest of the analysis falls into disarray.
The statements should not be read as a horizontal inventory of concepts.<1>p. 716</1>
One starts from the qualification of the object and of the regime of enjoyment, without which the rest of the analysis falls into disarray.<1>p. 717</1>
Is this an immaterial object of consumption?

Entry into the regime requires four fields, all of them present. The first is the promised object, identified by the core functions that organize the legitimate expectation of enjoyment. The second is the sustained position of enjoyment, because the acquisition opens a place in the ecosystem, and not a delivery that is exhausted in an instant. The third is infrastructural governance, with internal criteria and executive mechanisms that shape the experience and distribute consequences, and trivial technical mediation is not enough. The fourth is the typical possibility of relevant degradation without total rupture, in which enjoyment still exists on paper but is downgraded, emptied or reconfigured.

Application is decided by these verifiable elements, and not by technological intuition or by automatic deference to the contract. Nor do the criteria depend on full access to algorithms, logs and internal rules. What is demonstrated is the governance relevant to the acquired utility and a stability sufficient to produce patterns of enjoyment and degradation.
[...] sufficient to produce patterns of enjoyment and of relevant degradation without total rupture of access.<1>p. 430</1>
The first field covered by the criteria is the promised object, understood as an enjoyment bundle.<1>p. 428</1>

It requires identifying which core functions organize the legitimate expectation of enjoyment and, consequently, delimiting which alterations can reach the core of the object even when the formal continuity of access is preserved.<1>p. 428</1>

The filter here is decisive, since the presence of technical mediation in the trivial sense is not enough. What matters is the existence of internal criteria and executive mechanisms that structurally shape the experience of enjoyment and distribute consequences to the consumer.<1>p. 428</1>
The fourth field is the typical possibility of relevant degradation without total rupture.<1>p. 429</1>

The task is to delimit the zone in which enjoyment continues to exist formally, but is downgraded, emptied or reconfigured so as to frustrate the core of the utility offered or to reorder the consumer's position in the ecosystem in terms incompatible with the promise that justified the acquisition.<1>p. 429</1>

Application is not decided by technological intuition or by automatic deference to the contract, but by the cumulative presence of verifiable elements of the regime, which makes it possible to stabilize a path of qualification.<1>p. 429</1>

Criteria of application cannot depend on full access to algorithms, logs and internal rules as a condition of possibility, since that would turn the IOC into an impracticable category, reserved for exceptional cases.<1>p. 429</1>
How to use this page

Each situation opens with a guide to handling it, covering the facts that usually come up, how to demonstrate them, the normative basis and the precautions. Then comes the framework, in five parts. The parameter is the criterion that organizes the reading of the case. The normative basis is the legal rule on which the claim rests. The consequence is what can be sought, depending on the case.

The CDC functions as the normative infrastructure of these situations. The point is not to invent a new code or to graft a foreign regime onto the statutory text, but to read the categories of the system through the real way supply happens, in which governing the environment is governing enjoyment itself.

The framework does not mechanize the decision. It organizes the path from the governance structure to the duty breached, the minimum evidentiary requirement, the legal qualification and the possible consequence.

The minimum proof of each situation indicates what makes the conflict demonstrable with possible proof and controllable inferences, so that the discussion does not depend on full access to the platform's algorithms, records and internal rules.

It organizes, in consultable language, the passage between governance structure, duty breached, minimum evidentiary requirement, legal qualification and possible institutional consequence.<1>p. 748</1>
For the IOC, the criteria must operate with possible proof and controllable inferences<1>p. 429</1>
The point is not to invent a new code or to graft, by force, a foreign regime onto the statutory text.<1>p. 549</1>

Brazilian consumer law already contains, in its own architecture, sufficient instruments to reach immaterial, continuous forms of enjoyment governed by a third party, provided that its categories are read in light of the real way in which supply is rendered<1>p. 549</1>

The CDC already offers sufficient language to confront this problem, provided one accepts that, in continuous digital consumption, governing the environment is governing enjoyment itself.<1>p. 550</1>

When what was bought depends on the environment the platform administers
<1>a)</1> regime of governed enjoyment and application of the IOC
Which facts indicate a product that depends on the environment?

An item, account, subscription or access whose utility can be realized only inside the platform's environment, with loss of access, permanence or intelligibility, or with a change in the experience through an update. The supplier's typical defense is that it provides only a service or that it granted a mere content license. In games, the object may be one of appearance, progression, access and permanence, functionality, time or reputation, and a single item often combines more than one of these types. This typology is internal to the games laboratory, and not a general classification of platforms. The same traits appear in three business models, games operated as a service, marketplaces and artificial intelligence services supplied by platforms. In all of them, enjoyment depends on the continuous operation of a privately governed environment. In the marketplace, however, not every digital mediation turns the good into an immaterial object of consumption.
How do you demonstrate dependence on the environment?

The structural dependence of the utility on the governed environment, the way the experience is made available and the consumer's concrete position in the relationship. Helpful evidence includes the terms of use that tie the content to the account, the status page that shows dependence on servers and the record of what is in the account and what was paid.
What legal provision underpins the immaterial product?

Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Brazilian Consumer Protection Code (CDC)<1><2>1</2></1> already admits immaterial products. Whenever the utility consumed presents itself as a position of enjoyment sustained by continuous private governance, there is an immaterial product within the meaning of that provision, and the service dimension does not rule out control over enjoyment. Terms of use that recognize virtual content associated with the account, such as currency, skins and other items, help prove that the object exists, but they do not exhaust its regime. The IOC does not replace the immaterial product of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<3><4>1</4></3>. It gives that product concrete form in continuous and governed consumption. The legal definition of product works as a scope clause, which keeps protection from being evaded when the object has no physical medium.
What stays outside the entry gate?

The four fields of the entry gate are cumulative. Left out are one-off access, the platform that works only as a channel or storefront, the predominantly aesthetic alteration when the symbolic element is accessory and the ordinary variations of the service. There are also conflicts the CDC already resolves with nothing gained by invoking the IOC, such as undue charges, an isolated defect or a specific breach of an offer, when that is the core of the case. Qualification opens the following filters and does not decide the case on its own. Arguing over whether the case concerns a product or a service does not settle the question. The distinction remains useful for calibrating specific consequences, but it does not define the entire regime. The Legal Framework for Electronic Games, Law 14,852/2024, recognizes the sector as an economic and cultural activity, but the sectoral framing helps one see the market and is not enough to control governance, so it does not replace the CDC. The interpretive rule is that initial delivery does not exhaust performance, and continued performance does not erase the object.

The possible institutional consequence consists in opening the subsequent filters of the regime, preventing the controversy from being neutralized by the claim that there is a mere provision of services or simply a formal license<1>p. 743</1>

The contractual discipline of the service itself gives shape to this arrangement by establishing that access to the Services, including the so-called Virtual Content, is granted through a limited and revocable license, conditioned on compliance with the Terms, and that termination of the account entails automatic cancellation of the license and loss of access to the associated content<1>p. 408</1>

When it applies
When the utility consumed depends structurally on an environment that private governance administers, modulates and can change, with an impact on access, permanence, intelligibility or updating.

Whenever the utility consumed depends structurally on an environment administered, modulated and changeable by private governance, with an impact on access, permanence, intelligibility or updating of the experience, the IOC's field of application will be established.
Duty of supply
To ensure accessible, intelligible and preserved enjoyment, within the limits of the legitimate mutability of the environment.
The corresponding duty of supply is to ensure functionally accessible, intelligible and preserved enjoyment within the limits of the legitimate mutability of the environment.
Minimum proof
The dependence of the utility on the ecosystem, the way the experience is made available and the consumer's concrete position in the relationship.

The minimum proof required falls on demonstrating the structural dependence of the utility on the governed ecosystem, the way the experience is made available and the consumer's concrete position in the relationship.
Legal qualification
Immaterial product under Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. The service dimension of the relationship does not rule out control over enjoyment.

The resulting legal qualification is that of an immaterial product subject to the regime of art. 3, § 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, without the service dimension of the relationship ruling out control over enjoyment as the core of supply.
Institutional consequence
The following filters open, and the claim that there is mere service provision or a simple license no longer neutralizes the controversy.

The possible institutional consequence consists in opening the subsequent filters of the regime, preventing the controversy from being neutralized by the claim that there is a mere provision of services or simply a formal license.

When the consumer only understands what the interface lets them understand
<1>b)</1> semiotic vulnerability and governance of meaning
Which facts show meaning governed by the supplier?

Expectation, perception of value, risk assessment or capacity to contest that depend on signs, interfaces and trails controlled by the supplier. The simplest case is a purchase advertised in the storefront as an acquisition and characterized in the contract as a revocable license.
How do you reconstruct the consumer's journey?

The reconstruction of the user's journey, the informational architecture, the communicational salience and the paths of understanding. Useful evidence includes dated screenshots, screen recordings and the purchase, acceptance and confirmation screens, with the messages about rarity, time remaining and discounts. The claim is no longer that the consumer did not understand but that the environment was designed in a certain way.
Which rules deal with vulnerability and information?

Article 4, item I, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1> recognizes the consumer's vulnerability, which takes its own form in digital environments. Article 6 of the CDC<3><4>3</4></3> guarantees adequate information, protection against misleading advertising and facilitation of the consumer's defense, and Article 39, item IV, of the CDC<5><6>4</6></5> prohibits taking advantage of the consumer's weakness.
Is semiotic vulnerability presumed?

Semiotic vulnerability is not a generic attribute of the digital, and it does not presume the consumer's incapacity. It requires a governance of meaning that acts structurally on understanding, comparability, predictability or contestation. Combined with other elements, it may ground the redistribution of the burden of proof. The expression digital vulnerability names the setting in which the harm occurs, but it does not isolate the mechanism. Semiotic vulnerability targets the unequal administration of meaning and, for that reason, gives proof a sounder framework and better prepares the remedy. It is not a psychological trait of the consumer but a structural mechanism of power.

The first source of support is interface trails and decision flow: dated screenshots, screen recordings, purchase, acceptance, upgrade and confirmation screens, messages about rarity, equivalence, time remaining, discount, event or alteration<1>p. 607</1>
The claim is no longer “I did not understand” but “the environment was designed this way”.<1>p. 607</1>

From this perspective, it is argued that the consumer's factual vulnerability, expressly recognized in art. 4, I, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, takes on a form of its own in digital environments, tied to mediation by signs, interfaces and private criteria of visibility and enjoyment<3>p. 34</3>

The basic rights of the consumer, in turn, include adequate and clear information, protection against misleading and abusive advertising, prevention and redress of harm, and facilitation of the defense of their rights<1>p. 511</1>

[...] the discipline of quality defects that render the service unfit or diminish its value and the prohibition of abusive practices that take advantage of the consumer's weakness, impose excessive advantage or leave performance of the obligation to the exclusive discretion of the supplier<1>p. 520</1>

It is not enough that the case involves an interface, an algorithm or an online environment. The governance of meaning must act structurally on the understanding, comparability, predictability or contestation of enjoyment.<1>p. 721</1>

The possible legal qualification may sustain an abusive practice, informational insufficiency, deceptiveness through ambiguity or relevant omission and, when combined with other elements, a basis for the dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof<1>p. 744</1>
It names the environment in which the harm occurs, but does not isolate the legally relevant mechanism of the asymmetry.<1>p. 584</1>
The category targets a mechanism, not a setting.<1>p. 588</1>
The legally relevant problem becomes the unequal administration of meaning<1>p. 588</1>

Thus, semiotic vulnerability is not to be confused with a psychological trait of the consumer, a generic synonym for digital fragility or a mere environmental description of networked life. It is a structural mechanism of power<1>p. 501</1>

<1>p. 744</1> Whenever expectation, perception of value, risk assessment or capacity to contest depend on signs, interfaces, flows and informational trails controlled by the supplier, there will be legally relevant semiotic vulnerability.
Not to organize the experience through an asymmetry of meaning incompatible with good faith, transparency and the legibility of enjoyment.
The corresponding duty is not to organize the experience through a structural asymmetry of meaning incompatible with good faith, transparency and the legibility of enjoyment.
The user's journey, the informational architecture, the communicational salience, the paths of understanding and the records that make it possible to reconstruct how the expectation was formed.

The minimum proof required involves reconstructing the user's journey, the informational architecture of the environment, the communicational salience, the paths of understanding and the records available to reconstruct how the expectation was formed.
Possible legal qualification
Abusive practice, informational insufficiency, deceptiveness through ambiguity or relevant omission. Combined with other elements, it supports the dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof.

The possible legal qualification may sustain an abusive practice, informational insufficiency, deceptiveness through ambiguity or relevant omission and, when combined with other elements, a basis for the dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof.
The conflict is brought back to the governance of the environment, without moralizing the consumer's conduct, and reinforced duties of information, advertising and proof apply.

The institutional consequence consists in bringing the conflict back to the governance of the environment, avoiding moralization of the consumer's conduct and allowing reinforced duties of information, advertising and proof to apply.

When the information exists but gets buried in excess
<1>c)</1> inadequate information as functional opacity
Which facts show information that exists but offers no guidance?

Textual excess, strategic dispersion, fragmentation of informational paths and merely performative transparency. Essential rules sit in long documents, cross-references, FAQs and update histories that the consumer can hardly locate and connect to the impact they suffered.
How do you demonstrate that the meaning was not knowable?
What was shown, at what moment, with what salience and through which channels, and whether that organization allowed the consumer to understand what was relevant to join, stay or react.
Which rules require clear and conspicuous information?

Article 31 of the CDC<1><2>5</2></1> requires correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information in the offer and in the presentation. Article 46 of the CDC<3><4>6</4></3> releases the consumer from obligations when there was no real opportunity to learn of them beforehand or when the wording hinders understanding. Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 54 of the CDC<5><6>7</6></5> require clear adhesion contracts and highlighted limiting clauses. Article 47 of the CDC<7><8>8</8></7> requires clauses to be interpreted in the way most favorable to the consumer. This rule connects to the control of abusiveness provided for in Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<9><10>9</10></9>.
Is it enough to prove that the text was there?

The decisive point is not to prove that the text was there, but to assess whether the legally relevant meaning was knowable in real terms. Depending on the case, the failure qualifies as an informational quality defect, as an abusive practice by obscuring or as a basis for the invalidity of clauses.
The offer and presentation of products or services must ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information<1>p. 601</1>

Likewise, consumer contracts do not bind the consumer when they are not given a real opportunity to learn of the content beforehand, nor when they are drafted so as to hinder understanding of their meaning and scope<1>p. 601</1>

This is precisely what art. 54, under paragraphs 3 and 4, of the CDC makes explicit. Adhesion contracts must be drafted in clear terms, with conspicuous and legible characters, so as to facilitate their understanding, and clauses limiting rights must be drafted with prominence, allowing immediate and easy understanding<1>p. 621</1>
Contractual clauses shall be interpreted in the manner most favorable to the consumer.<1>p. 511</1>

For this reason, the new function of contract law places the principle of interpretation in accordance with good faith back at the center, so that art. 47 of the CDC<1><2>8</2></1>, together with the general clause of art. 51, IV, allows the pre-drafted clauses to be interpreted<3>p. 605</3>
The decisive point, therefore, lies not in proving that “the text was there”, but in assessing whether the legally relevant meaning was knowable in real terms.<1>p. 601</1>
When legibility is replaced by textual excess, strategic dispersion, fragmented informational paths or merely performative transparency.

Whenever the platform replaces legibility with textual excess, strategic dispersion, fragmentation of informational paths or merely performative transparency, there will be inadequate performance of the duty to inform.
To provide information that is materially adequate, useful for the decision and verifiable later, in case of controversy.
The corresponding duty of supply is to provide information that is materially adequate, useful for the decision and verifiable later, should a dispute arise.
What was shown, when, with what salience, through which channels and to what extent this allowed the consumer to understand what was relevant to join, stay or react.

The minimum proof required calls for identifying what was shown, at what moment, with what salience, through which channels and to what extent this organization allowed the consumer to understand what was legally relevant to join, stay or react.
Informational quality defect, abusive practice by functional obscuring and, depending on the case, invalidity of clauses or limitations incompatible with the expectation formed.

The legal qualification tends to apply as an informational quality defect of supply, an abusive practice by functional obscuring and, depending on the case, support for the invalidity of clauses or limitations incompatible with the legitimately formed expectation.
Correction of the communicational arrangement, reinforcement of useful transparency, disclosure orders and restoration of the affected enjoyment.

The possible institutional consequence includes a duty to correct the communicational arrangement, reinforcement of useful transparency, disclosure orders and restoration of the enjoyment affected by decisional opacity.
<1>Information, advertising and anticipation, on the jurist's path</1> · <2>The parameter</2><3> · <4>Statement 7.1.1.3 in the thesis</4></3>
When the storefront promised more than was delivered
<1>d)</1> advertising and offer as controllable management of expectation
Which facts show advertising inside the offer?

Enjoyment preceded by curated cycles of anticipation, promise, suggested scarcity, symbolic distinction or insinuated equivalences. A typical case is an item sold as exclusive that later reappears in an alternative store, in a special currency or at a much lower price, although the time limit of the exclusivity was never disclosed in an understandable way at the time of purchase.
How do you connect the promise to the later enjoyment?

The promotional environment, the communication pieces, the symbolic salience, the context in which the object is presented and the relation between the prior promise and the later enjoyment. Useful evidence includes promotional pieces, posts, campaigns, influencers, notices, asterisks, cascading cross-references and fine print. The questions are how the expectation was produced, at what moment the relevant conditions were revealed, with what prominence they appeared, what the sequence between promise and acceptance was and whether there were real means to understand and compare the offer.
Which rules make the offer binding?

Article 30 of the CDC<1><2>10</2></1> makes all sufficiently precise information binding, and the presentation in the digital storefront may constitute an offer. Article 35 of the CDC<3><4>11</4></3> allows the consumer to demand specific performance, accept an equivalent performance or rescind the contract and claim damages. Article 38 of the CDC<5><6>12</6></5> places on whoever sponsors the advertising the burden of proving that the information is true and correct. In the curated anticipation of the offer, relevant omission appears when what is essential is moved outside the focus of the decision. Advertising is misleading when the utility or equivalence built by the promotional environment finds no verifiable correspondence in enjoyment. And it is abusive when the design systematically exploits vulnerability, compressing deliberation through artificial urgency, symbolic reward and fragmentation of the relevant conditions.
Is insistent advertising enough?

Insistent advertising is not enough. What counts is the link between the prior promise and the later enjoyment. Communication becomes an element of abusive teleology only when it is tied to a broader exploitative program. Not every persuasion technique is unlawful, because the market may promote, dramatize and organize interest. But unlawfulness may lie in the way elements that seem neutral on their own are combined, and not only in a false advertisement or an isolated clause.

If, after a period, the same item reappears in an alternative store, in a special currency, in an aggressive promotion or at a significantly lower price, and if the time limitation of the exclusivity was not disclosed in an adequate and understandable way at the time of acquisition, there is a retroactive reconfiguration of the value delivered, with frustration of legitimate expectation and violation of transparency.<1>p. 214</1>
Promotional pieces, posts, campaigns, influencers, disclaimers, asterisks, cascading cross-references and fine print serve to map how the expectation was produced<1>p. 607</1>
All sufficiently precise information becomes part of the contract and binds the supplier<1>p. 562</1>
which supports reading the digital storefront as a binding offer<1>p. 433</1>
Hence the importance of art. 35 of the CDC<1><2>11</2></1><3>p. 540</3>
which allows the consumer to demand specific performance of the obligation, accept an equivalent performance or terminate the contract with losses and damages<1>p. 540</1>

It is precisely for this reason that art. 38 of the CDC<1><2>12</2></1> proves so important here. The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication lies with whoever sponsors it<3>p. 627</3>

The conduct may be legally qualified as misleading or abusive advertising, a binding offer, an abusive practice through administered ambiguity and, when tied to a broader exploitative program, an element of abusive teleology<1>p. 745</1>

The jurist must ask how the expectation was produced, at what moment the relevant conditions were revealed, with what prominence they appeared, what the actual sequence between promise and acceptance was<1>p. 633</1>
Relevant omission appears when the essential is deliberately moved outside the decisional focus.<1>p. 631</1>

Misleading advertising, in turn, manifests itself when the image of utility or equivalence built by the promotional environment finds no verifiable correspondence in the actual experience of enjoyment<1>p. 631</1>

Abusive advertising, finally, appears when the design of the environment systematically exploits the consumer's vulnerability, compressing their space for deliberation through artificial urgency, symbolic reward, ritualization of acceptance and fragmentation of the relevant conditions.<1>p. 631</1>
The market may promote, persuade, dramatize and organize interest.<1>p. 631</1>
In contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, unlawfulness may reside precisely in the combination of elements that, seen separately, seem neutral<1>p. 632</1>
When enjoyment is preceded by curated cycles of anticipation, promise, suggested scarcity, symbolic distinction or insinuated equivalences. Advertising becomes a material part of the offer.

Whenever enjoyment is preceded by curated cycles of anticipation, promise, suggested scarcity, symbolic distinction or insinuated equivalences, advertising will become <1>p. 745</1> a material part of the offer.
Ensuring correspondence between the promise, the announced value, the concealed costs and the experience actually made available.
The corresponding duty of supply is to ensure correspondence between promise, announced value, concealed costs and the experience actually made available under administered mutability.
The promotional environment, the communication pieces, the symbolic salience, the context of presentation and the relation between the promise and the later enjoyment.

The minimum proof required involves reconstructing the promotional environment, the communication pieces, the symbolic salience, the context in which the object was presented and the relation between prior promise and later enjoyment.
Misleading or abusive advertising, binding offer, abusive practice through administered ambiguity and, within a broader exploitative program, an element of abusive teleology.

The conduct may be legally qualified as misleading or abusive advertising, a binding offer, an abusive practice through administered ambiguity and, when tied to a broader exploitative program, an element of abusive teleology.
Correction of the offer, functional restoration, inhibitory relief over the communication and, depending on the case, invalidation of promotional strategies incompatible with what was delivered.

The possible institutional consequence covers correction of the offer, functional restoration, inhibitory relief over the communication and, depending on the case, invalidation of promotional strategies incompatible with the real experience delivered.

When the platform changed the rules and left no trace
<1>e)</1> structural opacity and open auditability
Which facts show an alteration without a trace?

A relevant change in access, performance, utility, operating rules or sanctions without preserving minimum trails for reconstruction. Which records should be requested to reconstruct the alteration?

Essential logs, the history of relevant versions, sanction records, minimum operational justifications, context data and delimited technical elements, enough to make the dispute knowable. Elements attributable to the supplier and publicly retrievable are also useful, such as update records, stated reasons for changes, access policies and internal sanction criteria.
Where does the duty to leave a trace come from?

Open auditability is a parameter, and not an institution foreign to the system. Is the platform equated with the State?

No. Functional public relevance does not make the platform equivalent to the State, and Brazil's Consumer Protection Code (CDC) does not become a parallel constitution of digital life. The legal order already has frameworks for limiting it, such as the Constitution and the CDC, reconciled with the social function of property and with intellectual property.

The ten parameters organize how each case is read, one per situation, in the order in which the analysis proceeds. Each one states what it controls, what is not enough and where it leads.
What do the parameters resolve?

The conflict is not resolved by how the sector looks or by how familiar society is with the technology. The case must be brought back to parameters dense enough to stabilize expectations, guide proof and allow consistent consequences. They reduce reliance on the interpreter's subjective repertoire and curb the tendency to decide on vague impressions about innovation, technical complexity or freedom of enterprise. What decides is how the environment organizes private power, redistributes the capacity to understand and to contest, and produces relevant frictions in the consumption experience.
The digital condition, by itself, decides nothing.<1>p. 715</1>

In what order are they applied?

It sets the standard of proof suited to the structure of the conflict. It points to the possible dogmatic consequence. The sequence works as a safeguard, because it prevents both breaking the conflict down into isolated clauses and replacing legal analysis with a diffuse impression about technology.

In the order of the parameters, the qualification of the object and semiotic vulnerability come first. Information and advertising follow.
